approachQuestion.prompt:
Route the Packages

Arrays payload and destination both have length n. destination is guaranteed to be a permutation of 0..n−1. For every index i, move payload[i] to index destination[i] in a new result array, and return that array. Equal payload values are allowed.

Example 1: payload=[10,20,30], destination=[2,0,1] → [20,30,10].
Example 2: payload=[7,7], destination=[1,0] → [7,7].
Example 3: payload=[9], destination=[0] → [9].

Constraints:
1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; payload values are integers between −10^9 and 10^9.
destination contains each index 0..n−1 exactly once. No validation of this guarantee is required.
Do not modify either input. Result must have its own storage.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; payload values are integers between −10^9 and 10^9.
destination contains each index 0..n−1 exactly once. No validation of this guarantee is required.

options.text: Allocate a result of length n. For each source index i, write result[destination[i]]=payload[i].
options.feedback: The permutation guarantee gives exactly one source for every destination, so all result positions are assigned once without overwriting needed inputs.

options.text: Build a separate inverse index array with inverse[destination[i]]=i. Allocate result and set result[j]=payload[inverse[j]] for every j.
options.feedback: This is correct, but the inverse array is removable when values can be written straight to their destinations.

options.text: Allocate result and set result[i]=payload[destination[i]] for every i.
options.feedback: The given map sends sources to destinations; it is not the inverse. Example 1 would produce [30,10,20] instead of [20,30,10].

options.text: For i from left to right, assign payload[destination[i]]=payload[i], then return a copy of payload.
options.feedback: This violates input preservation and can destroy a value needed later. For payload=[1,2], destination=[1,0], the first write loses the original 2.

feedback.reason: The map sends source positions to destinations: write result[destination[i]]=source[i].
details: Allocate one result array. Visit source positions in order and write each source value into its specified destination. The guaranteed permutation fills every slot exactly once.

The map sends source positions to destinations: write result[destination[i]]=source[i]. Using it as the inverse would move the wrong payload. The promised bijection ensures every destination is assigned once, including fixed points, without checking or reconstructing the permutation.

“Allocate a result of length n. For each source index i, write result[destination[i]]=payload[i].”: The permutation guarantee gives exactly one source for every destination, so all result positions are assigned once without overwriting needed inputs.

“Build a separate inverse index array with inverse[destination[i]]=i. Allocate result and set result[j]=payload[inverse[j]] for every j.”: This is correct, but the inverse array is removable when values can be written straight to their destinations.
“Allocate result and set result[i]=payload[destination[i]] for every i.”: The given map sends sources to destinations; it is not the inverse. Example 1 would produce [30,10,20] instead of [20,30,10].

“For i from left to right, assign payload[destination[i]]=payload[i], then return a copy of payload.”: This violates input preservation and can destroy a value needed later. For payload=[1,2], destination=[1,0], the first write loses the original 2.

complexityQuestion.prompt: For the fixed method “Scatter Sources into Fresh Storage”, choose the tightest worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair. Let n be the common length. Allocation per slot, indexed reads and writes cost constant time. Include all allocation and copying time; exclude the input arrays and returned result. Include helper indices and stack. No hashing, recursion, inverse-map array or dynamic append is used.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 200,000; payload values are integers between −10^9 and 10^9.
destination contains each index 0..n−1 exactly once. No validation of this guarantee is required.
Do not modify either input. Result must have its own storage.

options.text: O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.

feedback.reason: Scatter n payloads directly into the returned array.
details: One result allocation and one scan handle n values. The result itself is excluded from auxiliary space; only an index and current values remain. Permutation validity is an input guarantee, not an extra validation step.
The option “O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: The direct scatter fills n slots with constant helper state.
The option “O(n) time, O(n) auxiliary space.”: This would count the excluded result or an unused inverse array.
The option “O(n log n) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: No sorting is performed or needed.
The option “O(1) time, O(1) auxiliary space.”: The result must contain all n payload values.
